---
title: "R11. Data ethics and personal data"
description: "The data ethics position, raising a concern, and personal data."
---

Analysis at NHSBSA uses data about people, and informs decisions that affect them. This page
covers data ethics, personal data, and what to record when one of the ethics questions raises a
concern.

## Data ethics

Analysis should be undertaken in line with legal and ethical obligations and any other relevant
public service codes of conduct.[^src-govs-010-principle-5]

The **Data and AI Ethics Framework** provides guidance on using data appropriately and responsibly
when planning, implementing and evaluating a policy or service.[^src-govs-010-section-6-1]

### Use the Data and AI Ethics Framework, not the title GovS 010 names

Government Functional Standard GovS 010: Analysis cites it as the **Data Ethics Framework**, which
is the 2020 edition. On 18 December 2025 it was retitled the **Data and AI Ethics Framework**. Its
scope was extended to AI and algorithmic technologies, and four principles were added. Use the
current framework.

It publishes a **self-assessment tool**. Use that rather than writing your own checklist.

Ethics is a design activity, not a compliance check at the end. The framework has seven principles,
and each one is a question worth asking before the work starts.

- **Transparency.** Could you explain to the people in the data what you did and why?
- **Accountability.** Who is answerable if this turns out to be wrong?
- **Fairness.** Could the analysis, or the decision it informs, affect some groups differently? Five
  questions turn that from open-ended into answerable. Who is **represented** in the data, and in
  what proportion? Who is **missing** from it altogether? Is any variable acting as a **proxy** for
  a protected or sensitive characteristic? Do **outcomes differ** across groups once you look? How
  much fairness work is **proportionate** to what this analysis decides? An exploratory count at
  Level 1 does not need a bias audit. A model that decides who is eligible for something does.
- **Privacy.** Is the data being used no more than the question requires? NHSBSA's Statistical Disclosure Control protocol is where this is already answered. [NHSBSA templates and documents](r2-templates-and-documents.qmd) lists the protocol with the other
  NHSBSA documents this playbook draws on. Follow them rather than this page: a disclosure control
  protocol summarised in a playbook is a protocol with two versions.
- **Environmental sustainability.** What does producing and running this analysis cost, and is that
  proportionate to what it is for? This matters most for repeated pipelines and for anything using
  large models.
- **Societal impact.** Who is affected by the decision this analysis informs, beyond the people in
  the data? This is a scoping question, so it belongs in
  [Phase 1, engagement and scoping](../01-engagement-and-scoping/index.qmd) as well
  as here.
- **Safety.** What harm could follow if this is wrong, misread, or used for something it was not
  built for?

Raise societal impact and safety at scoping, while there is still time to act on the answer.

Answer the accountability question first. If nobody can answer it, the governance is not yet in
place. See [roles and responsibilities](../06-roles/index.qmd).

### A gap in coverage is a fairness question {#a-gap-in-coverage-is-a-fairness-question}

At Level 2, [the checks by level](../07-deciding-your-assurance-level/what-your-level-requires.qmd#the-checks-by-level)
include an understanding of the impacts of data quality. The input data is profiled for ranges,
nulls, duplicates and outliers, and for what each means for the answer. That includes who is missing
from it.

A gap in coverage is not only a wider interval. It is a blind spot in the conclusion, because the
analysis cannot see the group that is missing. It is also a risk of affecting one group differently.

Fairness asks who is missing from the data altogether, as one of its five questions.
[Uncertainty, assumptions and limitations](r10-uncertainty.qmd#limitations) covers the uncertainty
side, where a gap in coverage limits what the figures can be used for.

## When a question raises something {#when-a-question-raises-something}

Where one of the seven questions raises a concern, record the concern and what you decided about it,
rather than leaving it in an email.

**Record six things.** They fit in a short block in the project record. They are the same six
whether the concern is fairness, privacy, safety or societal impact.

| Field | What goes in it |
|---|---|
| **Affected groups** | Who is affected by this, in the data and beyond it |
| **Harms and benefits** | What could go wrong, and what the analysis is for. Record both |
| **Mitigations** | What you actually changed: the method, the caveat, the scope, the publication decision |
| **Residual risk** | What is still there after the mitigations, stated plainly rather than implied by silence |
| **Accountable decision-maker** | The role that accepted that residual risk. Not the analyst, unless the analyst genuinely holds that authority |
| **Escalation route** | Where it went, if the analyst and the commissioner could not settle it between them |

: The six fields to record for a concern, and what goes in each

Record the six fields whether or not the concern was settled. Six lines in the project record is
enough.

### Where an ethical concern goes if it is not settled

A design and plan should cover escalation routes that let analysts and stakeholders raise
concerns.[^src-govs-010-section-5-3]

Take it to the commissioner first, because they own the decision the analysis informs. This is the
same route as in [roles and responsibilities](../06-roles/index.qmd). Unresolved, it goes to the
**Analytical Quality and Assurance Lead**.

Where the concern is about something that will be published as an official statistic, it goes
to the **Lead Official for Statistics**. That is already the route for whether an output is fit
to publish.

**Refusing to do a piece of analysis is a legitimate outcome of this route**, and it is not the
analyst's alone to take. That is what the accountable decision-maker field is for.

## Personal data

Where personal data is used in analysis, this must be in accordance with NHSBSA policy and
prevailing legislation. GovS 010 says the same, as a recommendation: the use should be in accordance with the organisation's policies and prevailing legislation.[^src-govs-010-section-6-14]

Where analysis using personal data is published, you may include in the publication:[^src-govs-010-section-6-14]

- when personal data has been used, and the justification for its use
- how guidance has been followed
- the steps taken to protect the data

Information and data should be classified and securely managed in line with GovS 007 Security. They
should also be retained to meet statutory and contractual requirements, and those of the Data and AI
Ethics Framework.[^src-govs-010-section-6-7]

**Ask before the work starts, not at sign-off.** Information governance advice, and the corporate
data protection impact assessment (DPIA) process, sit with the information governance function.
Ask your team lead, or use the routes in [who to ask](r3-who-to-ask.qmd), to start a DPIA.

Go there while the question is still what data to use. A data protection impact assessment raised
after the analysis is built is a review of a decision already taken.
